ranked_papers.title: CDK4/6-targeted therapy for gastrointestinal cancers: from resistance mechanisms to immuno-combination strategies guided by biomarkers.
ranked_papers.authors: Cui J, Zhang Y, Wu Y, Zhang G, Lan J, Wang Y.
ranked_papers.abstract: Gastrointestinal (GI) cancers, encompassing esophageal, gastric, colorectal, hepatocellular, and pancreatic cancers, represent a major global health burden with persistently high morbidity and mortality. Given the limited therapeutic options and poor prognoses for patients with advanced-stage disease, there is an urgent and unmet clinical need for novel targeted therapies. Cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors (such as palbociclib, ribociclib, and abemaciclib) exert their effects by arresting the cell cycle at the G1/S checkpoint. Their landmark clinical success in hormone receptor-positive breast cancer has highlighted the therapeutic potential of targeting cell cycle regulation, thereby prompting extensive investigation into their application in solid tumors of the digestive system. Emerging evidence indicates that, beyond their direct antiproliferative effects, CDK4/6 inhibitors profoundly remodel the tumor immune microenvironment (TIME). By enhancing tumor antigen presentation, diminishing the immunosuppressive activity of regulatory T cells (Tregs), and promoting effector T cell infiltration, these agents provide a robust mechanistic rationale for synergistic combinations with immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). However, the frequent dysregulation of the CDK4/6-RB pathway and the inherently complex TIME in digestive cancers often precipitate primary and acquired drug resistance, which restricts their clinical efficacy. Consequently, elucidating the mechanisms that modulate drug sensitivity and developing biomarker-driven combination regimens have become critical research priorities. This review systematically summarizes the mechanisms governing the sensitivity of digestive tract tumors to CDK4/6 inhibitors. From the perspective of laboratory medicine, we further emphasize the importance of biomarker detection, therapeutic target assessment, and precision molecular subtyping in identifying patients most likely to benefit from CDK4/6 inhibitor-based therapies. In addition, we discuss the role of these agents in remodeling the TIME, evaluate current combination strategies aimed at overcoming resistance, and highlight future directions for advancing this rapidly evolving field.
ranked_papers.relevance_reason: Focuses on CDK4/6-targeted therapy resistance mechanisms in GI cancers; no substantive discussion of p53 mutations or their molecular effects.

ranked_papers.title: Cyclin-Dependent Kinases 4 and 6 Inhibitors: An Emerging Therapeutic Framework from Growth Suppression to Tumor Clearance.
ranked_papers.authors: Ma C, Ji X, Huang W, Guo S, Wang L, Wu X, Zheng H, Wang J.
ranked_papers.abstract: This review explores strategies to overcome the clinical limitations of Cyclin-dependent kinases 4 and 6 (CDK4/6) inhibitors, namely, reversible cytostasis and acquired resistance. We outline an emerging therapeutic framework in which these inhibitors induce specific vulnerabilities, shifting the treatment objective from growth suppression toward tumor clearance. Specifically, we analyze the effects of CDK4/6 inhibitors across four interconnected domains: cellular senescence, compromised DNA damage repair, metabolic reprogramming, and immune microenvironment remodeling. Building upon this framework, we summarize rational combination strategiessuch as pairing with senolytics, poly-(ADP-ribose) polymerase (PARP) inhibitors, or immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs)designed to exploit these induced vulnerabilities. To bridge preclinical rationale with clinical application, we discuss key translational determinants, noting that successful implementation depends on biomarker-guided patient selection and optimized dosing schedules (e.g., sequential administration) to mitigate overlapping toxicities. Collectively, the evidence suggests that rational combination strategies could repurpose CDK4/6 inhibitor therapy for more durable tumor control.
ranked_papers.relevance_reason: Reviews CDK4/6 inhibitor therapeutic strategies; no mention of p53 mutations or molecular mechanisms of p53 dysfunction.

ranked_papers.title: ERKed by too much signaling: from oncogenic driver to therapeutic vulnerability.
ranked_papers.authors: Farnsworth DA, Naznin F, Subramaniam A, Sew K, Lockwood WW.
ranked_papers.journal: Cellular and molecular life sciences : CMLS
ranked_papers.abstract: Extracellular regulated kinase (ERK) signaling is a major driver of cancer development. Mutations accumulated in oncogenes upstream of ERK can promote and sustain tumorigenesis by providing a sustained proliferative signal, helping cells resist death, and inducing angiogenesis. Therapeutic strategies for cancers with dysregulated ERK signaling have focused on inhibiting upstream-mutated oncogenes as a means of depriving tumors of these essential survival cues. While these strategies have demonstrated initial clinical success in patients, they also represent an incomplete understanding of the more nuanced role ERK signaling plays in tumor cell homeostasis. It is now understood that increased ERK signaling can also function as a tumor suppressor by inducing proliferative arrest outside of the framework of oncogene-induced senescence. In this review, we highlight current research describing the vulnerability of cancer cells to ERK hyperactivation induced toxicity and offer insight on how ERK rewiring may be leveraged for the development of new therapeutic strategies for patients.
ranked_papers.relevance_reason: Focuses on ERK signaling in oncogenesis and therapeutic vulnerability; no discussion of p53 mutations or their molecular effects.

selected_papers.title: Evaluation of non-canonical p53 functions in DNA replication and recombination for variant classification.
selected_papers.authors: Jansche R, Heitmeir B, Faust U, Pospiech H, Sutter C, Albig C, Hennig F, Janni W, Schmutzler R, Hauke J, Joerger AC, Wiesmüller L.
selected_papers.abstract: Pathogenic germline TP53 variants predispose to diverse Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS) phenotypes and a broad cancer spectrum, whereby carriers of hypomorphic variants cluster in a cohort with attenuated disease onset and an overrepresentation of breast cancer (BC). Recently, functional assays have gained importance among the criteria used to predict the pathogenicity of hereditary breast and ovarian cancer (HBOC) risk-gene variants. Experimental assays scoring p53 functions in transcription and growth control have contributed to variant classification, yet a significant fraction of TP53 variants remain of unknown significance (VUS). To understand whether non-canonical functions of p53 in the fidelity control of DNA replication may aid variant classification, we subjected 23 TP53 VUS and 20 control variants identified in the German Consortium for HBOC (GC-HBOC) to assays that monitor nascent DNA synthesis and recombination-mediated bypass of replication barriers. Our results reveal a clear functional separation between benign (B)/likely benign (LB) and pathogenic (P)/likely pathogenic (LP) variants in recombination measurements, with B/LB variants associated with high recombination frequencies and P/LP variants with low recombination frequencies. Importantly, 8/23 VUS exhibited activities within the B/LB or P/LP ranges and therefore emerge as candidates for revised classification. Variant-specific recombination activities showed significant correlations with functional scores from four earlier studies systematically analyzing canonical p53 functions. Differently, in DNA fiber spreading assays B/LB and P/LP variants showed a more heterogeneous pattern and thus did not consistently recapitulate replication slow-down and acceleration observed in the presence and absence of p53, respectively. Structural modeling of separation-of-function (SOF) variants in transcription and recombination indicates varying effects on protein stability and the conformation of surface-exposed regions, affecting for example, the flexibility of Loop 1 (L1). Intriguingly, individual SOF variants suggest that loss-of-function (LOF) in recombination may drive BC, underscoring the predictive power of this assay for low-penetrance TP53 variants.
selected_papers.relevance_reason: Directly examines pathogenic TP53 variants, using functional assays (transcription, recombination, DNA replication) and structural modeling to show how disease-associated mutations affect protein stability and conformation, providing mechanistic insight into loss/separation-of-function.

selected_papers.title: p53: from understanding its structure to advances in therapeutic targeting.
selected_papers.authors: Wang W, Liu X, Liu H, Abolhassani H, Yan H, Zhang H, Wang X.
selected_papers.abstract: The tumor suppressor gene TP53 is the most frequently mutated gene in human cancers and has been a popular area of research in the field of oncology. The p53 protein, encoded by the TP53 gene, not only binds to many targeted genes but also regulates apoptosis, autophagy, cell cycle arrest, metabolism, senescence and the tumor immune microenvironment to suppress tumorigenesis. In recent years, an increasing number of new functions of p53 have been discovered, and p53-mediated tumor suppressor functions have been greatly expanded. Mutations in TP53 not only abolish its ability to suppress tumorigenesis but also confer carcinogenic properties to p53-mutant cells. Because of the prevalence of p53 dysfunction in various disease types, p53 has long been considered an attractive target for new anticancer drugs. However, drugs targeting p53 are still under investigation in early clinical trials and have not been approved for clinical use. This finding is consistent with the speculation that p53 is widely regarded as "undruggable." Surprisingly, several novel therapeutic approaches targeting p53, including MDM2/4 antagonists, compounds that target specific p53 mutants or restore the wild-type function of the mutated p53 protein, p53-based genetic therapies and p53-based tumor immunotherapy, have been developed in recent years. Here, we present a review of the structure, inactivation, and roles of p53 in diseases. In addition, this review discusses the efforts to target diseases associated with p53 dysfunction and the challenges encountered in the clinical development of these approaches.
selected_papers.relevance_reason: Reviews p53 structure and how mutations abolish tumor suppressor function while conferring gain-of-function properties, directly addressing molecular disruption caused by disease-associated p53 mutations.

selected_papers.title: Restoration of the Y220C p53 Full-Length Mutant by PK11000: a Molecular Dynamics Study of an Intrinsically Disordered Protein.
selected_papers.authors: Stetson S, Caballero Mancía F, Thayer KM.
selected_papers.abstract: The tumor suppressor protein p53 plays a key role in cellular homeostasis, with its dysfunction linked to over half of all cases of human cancer. The Y220C mutation in the DNA-binding domain (DBD) destabilizes p53, compromising its function. The most well-studied case of Y220C p53 rescue via a small molecule, PK11000, has been shown to restore stability and reinstate activity both in vitro and in vivo in rodent models. While prior in silico studies have focused on the DBD in isolation, this work explores the full-length p53 protein, incorporating its intrinsically disordered N- and C-terminal regulatory regions, which are known to be sites of extensive post-translational modifications utilized to modulate its activity. Using molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, we investigate the wild-type (WT) p53, the destabilized Y220C mutant, and the PK11000-rescued Y220C variant. Our findings illuminate a multilayered allosteric landscape: the Y220C mutation disrupts DBD stability through long-range effects while PK11000 counteracts this destabilization through its own distal interactions. Importantly, the N- and C-terminal regions mediate additional allosteric regulation, dynamically influencing both the mutation's impact and the rescue mechanism. This triple allosteric framework underscores the regulatory regions' critical role in restoring p53 functionality. By providing a first-order exploration into the behavior of full-length p53, this study advances our understanding of its regulatory mechanisms and sets the stage for developing targeted therapies aimed at reactivating mutant p53 in cancer.
selected_papers.relevance_reason: Directly investigates the Y220C p53 mutation's molecular mechanism of destabilization via MD simulations, including allosteric effects on DBD stability and rescue by a small molecule, providing detailed mechanistic insight into how a disease-associated mutation disrupts p53 function.

selected_papers.title: <i>In vitro</i> screening of compounds for targeting gastric cancer with Y220C p53 mutation: a molecule combining zinc chelation and a Michael acceptor drives <i>CDKN1</i> and <i>BBC3</i> expression to restore a p53-dependent cytotoxicity.
selected_papers.authors: Nannini S, Sieffert C, McGown A, Gao XY, Jarvis A, Kostakis GE, Galvacsi A, Kallay C, Moraru R, Baud MG, Mandel S, Balourdas DI, Joerger AC, Orvain C, Peschard S, Nion A, Mellitzer G, Lottiaux S, Spencer J, Gross I, Gaiddon C.
selected_papers.journal: Journal of enzyme inhibition and medicinal chemistry
selected_papers.abstract: Point mutations in p53 favour tumour aggressivity, particularly in gastric cancer (GC), and offer a target for small molecule-based anticancer treatments. This study focused on the p53-Y220C mutation, which causes p53 misfolding due to thermal instability associated with the creation of a pocket that may accommodate small molecules. This mutation also creates an additional free cysteine thiol group that may react with Michael acceptors. Using an integrated in silico and in vitro approach, four compounds (AG1, AG2, AG3, and RK349) were screened for potential reactivation of p53-Y220C in GC cells. AG3, a compound with zinc chelation and Michael acceptor properties, was found to induce p53 target gene expression via p53-dependent and -independent pathways. AG3 limited reactive oxygen species production, reducing toxicity to healthy cells. Furthermore, AG3 induced p53-dependent cytotoxicity and enhanced chemotherapy response. This study presents a novel compound with p53-Y220C reactivation potential, highlighting its promise for further development.
selected_papers.relevance_reason: Examines the p53-Y220C mutation's molecular mechanism (misfolding, thermal instability, pocket formation) and tests small molecules for reactivation, directly addressing how a disease-associated mutation disrupts p53 function and how it might be rescued.

selected_papers.title: Targeting mutant p53 in cancer: from mechanistic insights to therapeutic strategies.
selected_papers.authors: Wu HH, Leng S, Eisenstat DD, Sergi C, Leng R.
selected_papers.abstract: The tumor suppressor p53, often referred to as the “guardian of the genome,” is mutated in more than half of human cancers. These mutations have a significant impact on cancer biology and response to therapy. p53 mutations involve a range of changes that interfere with DNA binding, eliminate tumor suppressor functions, and, in many cases, confer dominant-negative or gain-of-function characteristics that actively promote oncogenesis. These mutations are closely linked to poor clinical outcomes and resistance to standard treatments. This review examines the impact of p53 mutations on cancer therapy in various ways. In chemotherapy and radiotherapy, loss of wild-type p53 impairs DNA damage responses, whereas mutant forms often contribute to treatment resistance. Additionally, p53 status influences responses to targeted therapies and immunotherapies, thereby affecting patient outcomes and prognoses. Importantly, ongoing clinical trials are beginning to integrate p53 mutational status as a predictive biomarker for therapy selection. Strategies aimed at restoring p53 activity are gaining increasing popularity in the development of treatments. These approaches include gene therapy to reintroduce the wild-type gene, targeted degradation of mutant p53 proteins, and small molecules designed to refold or reactivate mutant p53. In addition, synthetic lethality frameworks are being utilized to exploit vulnerabilities specific to tumors with p53 mutations, as well as interventions that target downstream effectors of p53 pathway. Together, these strategies represent a significant shift in precision oncology.
selected_papers.relevance_reason: Directly addresses how p53 mutations disrupt DNA binding, eliminate tumor suppressor function, and confer dominant-negative or gain-of-function properties, providing mechanistic insight central to the question.

function: Multifunctional transcription factor that induces cell cycle arrest, DNA repair or apoptosis upon binding to its target DNA sequence (PubMed:11025664, PubMed:12524540, PubMed:12810724, PubMed:15186775, PubMed:15340061, PubMed:17317671, PubMed:17349958, PubMed:19556538, PubMed:20673990, PubMed:20959462, PubMed:22726440, PubMed:24051492, PubMed:24652652, PubMed:35618207, PubMed:36634798, PubMed:38653238, PubMed:9840937). Acts as a tumor suppressor in many tumor types; induces growth arrest or apoptosis depending on the physiological circumstances and cell type (PubMed:11025664, PubMed:12524540, PubMed:12810724, PubMed:15186775, PubMed:15340061, PubMed:17189187, PubMed:17317671, PubMed:17349958, PubMed:19556538, PubMed:20673990, PubMed:20959462, PubMed:22726440, PubMed:24051492, PubMed:24652652, PubMed:38653238, PubMed:9840937). Negatively regulates cell division by controlling expression of a set of genes required for this process (PubMed:11025664, PubMed:12524540, PubMed:12810724, PubMed:15186775, PubMed:15340061, PubMed:17317671, PubMed:17349958, PubMed:19556538, PubMed:20673990, PubMed:20959462, PubMed:22726440, PubMed:24051492, PubMed:24652652, PubMed:9840937). One of the activated genes is an inhibitor of cyclin-dependent kinases. Apoptosis induction seems to be mediated either by stimulation of BAX and FAS antigen expression, or by repression of Bcl-2 expression (PubMed:12524540, PubMed:17189187). Its pro-apoptotic activity is activated via its interaction with PPP1R13B/ASPP1 or TP53BP2/ASPP2 (PubMed:12524540). However, this activity is inhibited when the interaction with PPP1R13B/ASPP1 or TP53BP2/ASPP2 is displaced by PPP1R13L/iASPP (PubMed:12524540). In cooperation with mitochondrial PPIF is involved in activating oxidative stress-induced necrosis; the function is largely independent of transcription. Induces the transcription of long intergenic non-coding RNA p21 (lincRNA-p21) and lincRNA-Mkln1. LincRNA-p21 participates in TP53-dependent transcriptional repression leading to apoptosis and seems to have an effect on cell-cycle regulation. Implicated in Notch signaling cross-over. Prevents CDK7 kinase activity when associated to CAK complex in response to DNA damage, thus stopping cell cycle progression. Isoform 2 enhances the transactivation activity of isoform 1 from some but not all TP53-inducible promoters. Isoform 4 suppresses transactivation activity and impairs growth suppression mediated by isoform 1. Isoform 7 inhibits isoform 1-mediated apoptosis. Regulates the circadian clock by repressing CLOCK-BMAL1-mediated transcriptional activation of PER2 (PubMed:24051492)

research_brief.question: How do disease-associated mutations in p53 disrupt its function at the molecular level?
research_brief.answer: The supplied evidence converges on a multi-layered mechanistic picture in which disease-associated TP53 mutations disrupt p53 function through several non-mutually-exclusive molecular routes. First, mutations can directly impair DNA binding by the central DNA-binding domain (DBD), eliminating sequence-specific transactivation of target genes, as summarized generally in a review (41917811). This is structurally plausible given that UniProt curation identifies four DBD residues (C176, H179, C238, C242) as direct Zn(2+) coordination sites, and RCSB PDB contains numerous crystal structures of DBD hot-spot mutants (e.g., R273H, R273C, R249S, R282W, Y220C, G245S, V272M, N235K) many solved in complex with DNA or destabilizing/stabilizing small molecules, consistent with the concept that mutations in or near the zinc-binding/DNA-contacting region compromise structural integrity or direct DNA contact; however, the supplied evidence does not include primary functional or thermodynamic data linking these specific PDB structures to loss of DNA binding beyond their existence as structures. Second, some mutations act through long-range allosteric destabilization rather than purely local disruption: computational (MD simulation) evidence for the Y220C mutation indicates it destabilizes the DBD via long-range allosteric effects propagated through the protein, with the intrinsically disordered N- and C-terminal regions dynamically modulating both the mutation's impact and potential pharmacological rescue (41552434). Third, biochemical/structural rationale (presented as background in a covalent-inhibitor study) indicates that Y220C specifically causes thermal misfolding that opens a druggable surface pocket not present in wild-type p53, and introduces a reactive free cysteine thiol enabling covalent small-molecule engagement (42163716); this is corroborated indirectly by the large number of RCSB Y220C structures co-crystallized with pocket-binding and covalently-bound stabilizer molecules, though the PDB entries alone are structural metadata and do not independently establish the misfolding mechanism. Fourth, beyond canonical transcriptional loss-of-function, disease-associated (pathogenic/likely pathogenic) TP53 variants also show reduced non-canonical activity in a DNA recombination/replication-barrier bypass assay relative to benign variants, and structural modeling of separation-of-function variants suggests altered protein stability and flexibility of surface loops (e.g., Loop 1) can selectively impair recombination-associated function versus transcriptional function, with loss of recombination activity specifically correlating with a breast cancer phenotype in some variants (41764184). Fifth, at the whole-protein/cellular level, TP53 mutations are described broadly (in reviews) as not merely abolishing tumor-suppressive transcriptional programs governing apoptosis, cell cycle arrest, autophagy, senescence, metabolism, and immune microenvironment regulation, but also conferring dominant-negative interference with co-expressed wild-type p53 and gain-of-function oncogenic activities that actively promote tumorigenesis and treatment resistance (41917811, 41942427). Overall, the evidence supports a model in which p53 mutations disrupt function through: (a) direct structural/DNA-contact disruption in the DBD, (b) allosteric destabilization propagated across domains, (c) selective disruption of specific molecular functions (transcription vs. recombination) depending on mutation and structural context, and (d) conversion of the protein into a dominant-negative or gain-of-function oncoprotein—though most of this mechanistic detail comes from abstracts, reviews, or computational studies rather than direct primary biochemical/structural findings fully elaborated in the supplied text.

key_findings.finding: General TP53 mutations interfere with DNA binding, abolishing transcriptional tumor-suppressor activity.
TP53 mutations can confer dominant-negative effects over co-expressed wild-type p53.
TP53 mutations can confer gain-of-function oncogenic properties beyond loss of tumor suppression.
Y220C destabilizes the DBD through long-range allosteric effects, modulated by intrinsically disordered N- and C-terminal regions ('triple allosteric framework').
Y220C causes thermal misfolding creating a druggable pocket and an additional reactive free cysteine thiol not present in wild-type p53.

Pathogenic/likely pathogenic TP53 variants show low recombination-bypass activity distinct from benign variants, indicating disruption of a non-canonical DNA recombination/replication fidelity function.
Structural modeling suggests separation-of-function variants alter protein stability and Loop 1 flexibility, differentially affecting transcription versus recombination functions.
Loss of recombination function in specific separation-of-function variants correlates with breast cancer phenotype.
p53 dysfunction disrupts multiple downstream pathways: apoptosis, autophagy, cell cycle arrest, metabolism, senescence, and tumor immune microenvironment regulation.
UniProt curation identifies four DBD zinc-coordinating residues (C176, H179, C238, C242) essential to structural integrity relevant to many hot-spot mutation sites.

Numerous crystal structures of p53 DBD hot-spot mutants (R273H, R273C, R249S, R282W, Y220C, G245S, V272M, N235K, etc.), some bound to DNA or small-molecule stabilizers/covalent modifiers, exist in the PDB, consistent with structural studies of mutant destabilization and pharmacological rescue.

consensus: Disease-associated p53 mutations are consistently described as impairing normal transcriptional tumor-suppressor activity across review-level and mechanistic sources.
Multiple lines of evidence (computational and structural background) converge on the DBD, and specifically hot-spot residues such as Y220C, as a focal point of destabilization.
Both canonical transcriptional function and non-canonical functions (e.g., recombination/replication fidelity) can be disrupted by pathogenic mutations, though through distinct molecular routes.
Multiple sources agree that mutant p53 is not simply inactive but can acquire additional dominant-negative or gain-of-function properties.
uncertainties_and_disagreements: The abstracts provide only high-level mechanistic claims (e.g., 'long-range allosteric effects', 'interferes with DNA binding') without residue-level biochemical detail in most cases.

The Y220C misfolding/pocket-formation and thiol-reactivity claims from 42163716 are described as background context rather than as this study's direct experimental finding, per the provided limitations.
The separation-of-function variant structural modeling (41764184) does not specify which mutations were modeled, limiting mechanistic specificity.
It is unclear from the evidence how commonly dominant-negative versus gain-of-function mechanisms operate relative to simple loss-of-function across the mutation spectrum.

The large number of PDB structures for hot-spot mutants demonstrates that these mutants have been structurally characterized, but the supplied PDB metadata alone does not describe *how* each specific mutation alters structure or function without accompanying primary literature evidence.
evidence_gaps: No direct primary biochemical or structural data are provided (only background/computational or abstract-level claims) explaining precisely how most hot-spot DBD mutations disrupt Zn2+ coordination, DNA contact geometry, or dimer/tetramer interfaces.
No mechanistic detail is provided linking gain-of-function or dominant-negative p53 mutants to specific molecular partners or pathways.
The relationship between the recombination-assay-based separation-of-function findings and canonical transcriptional loss-of-function mechanisms is not mechanistically reconciled.

No data are supplied on oligomerization domain (tetramerization) mutations despite PDB structures of this domain being available, leaving a gap regarding disruption of p53 oligomerization as a mutation mechanism.

recommended_papers.reason: Provides the most detailed mechanistic (computational) insight into allosteric propagation of mutation effects across full-length p53.
Describes specific biochemical consequences (misfolding, pocket formation, reactive thiol) of the Y220C mutation relevant to structure-based drug design.
Introduces evidence for disruption of a non-canonical p53 function (recombination) by pathogenic variants, expanding the mechanistic scope beyond transcription.

research_brief.next_investigation: Directly compare biochemical/thermodynamic destabilization data (e.g., melting temperature, DNA-binding affinity, oligomerization state) across a panel of hot-spot DBD mutants (R175H, R248W, R273H, Y220C) alongside dominant-negative/gain-of-function cellular assays to establish which specific structural defect (local DNA-contact loss vs. global misfolding vs. allosteric destabilization) predominates for each mutation class.
research_brief.source_warning: All literature evidence originates from abstracts only, not full-text methods or results, and several claims (e.g., Y220C pocket formation, general DNA-binding disruption) are explicitly noted as background statements or review-level generalizations rather than primary experimental findings. The UniProt entry provides curated but generic residue-level annotation (Zn-binding sites) without mutation-specific mechanistic detail. The RCSB PDB list documents structural metadata (existence, method, resolution) for numerous p53 mutant structures but does not itself provide mechanistic interpretation; inferences about mutation effects from PDB entries alone are speculative unless supported by accompanying literature. Conclusions should be treated as a provisional synthesis pending review of full primary literature.
